stem: In a study of healthy men, fluid taken from the seminiferous tubules has a testosterone concentration about 100 times higher than that in blood. Most of the testosterone is made by cells between the tubules under LH stimulation, and FSH acts on the cells lining the tubules.
oneliner: Study of healthy men + tubular fluid testosterone ~100× blood + made by interstitial cells under LH + FSH acts on tubule lining cells → how does tubular testosterone stay so high?
ask: Which mechanism best explains the high testosterone concentration in the tubules?

options.C: FSH-stimulated binding of testosterone by androgen-binding protein from Sertoli cells
options.D: Binding to plasma sex hormone-binding globulin
options.E: Local conversion to DHT by Leydig cells

whyNot.A: Germ cells **do not make testosterone**; Leydig cells do
whyNot.B: **Inhibin B** feeds back on FSH; it does not bind testosterone
whyNot.D: SHBG carries hormone **in blood**, which would lower, not concentrate, tubular levels
whyNot.E: Leydig cells make testosterone, and **DHT is made in target tissue** by 5-alpha-reductase

why: **LH drives Leydig testosterone**; **FSH makes Sertoli cells secrete androgen-binding protein (ABP)**. ABP **binds testosterone inside the tubule** and holds the concentration high, which spermatogenesis needs.
chain: FSH stimulates Sertoli cells to make ABP
ABP binds testosterone in the tubule
High local testosterone for sperm production

idea.rule: LH feeds Leydig cells (testosterone); FSH feeds Sertoli cells (ABP, inhibin B); ABP keeps testosterone high where sperm are made.
also: Inhibin B from Sertoli cells inhibits FSH
Testosterone inhibits LH
Exogenous testosterone shuts off FSH/LH and lowers intratesticular testosterone, harming sperm

stem: A 38-year-old woman has noticed spots of blood on her bra from the left nipple for 3 weeks. Pressing at the 4 o'clock position brings out a drop of blood from one duct. There is no palpable mass, the nipple skin is normal, and her mammogram and serum prolactin are normal.
oneliner: 38F + 3 wk bloody discharge from one duct, left nipple + no mass + normal nipple skin, mammogram and prolactin → mechanism?
ask: Which mechanism best explains the discharge?

options.A: Fragile vessels within a papillary growth inside one lactiferous duct
options.C: Malignant cells spreading within the nipple epidermis
options.D: Rupture of a cyst in fibrocystic change
options.E: Bacterial infection of the breast ducts

whyNot.B: Prolactin is **normal**; discharge would be milky and bilateral
whyNot.C: **Paget disease**: scaly, eczematous nipple skin; skin is normal
whyNot.D: Gives **multiple lumps and green or clear fluid**, not blood from a single duct

why: A **papillary tumor with a fibrovascular core grows inside a lactiferous duct**. The **thin-walled vessels bleed easily**, giving **unilateral single-duct bloody discharge without a mass** and a normal mammogram.
chain: Blood drains out of the nipple

idea.rule: Bloody discharge from one duct without a mass is a papilloma until proven otherwise.
also: Milky bilateral discharge: prolactinoma, drugs
Multiple papillomas carry higher cancer risk
Intraductal carcinoma can also bleed, so imaging or biopsy is needed

stem: At 32 weeks of gestation, a routine ultrasound of a male fetus shows a thin rim of anechoic fluid around both testes within the scrotum. The testes lie in the scrotum, the bladder and kidneys look normal, and there is no bowel dilatation or calcification.
oneliner: Male fetus 32 wk + anechoic fluid around both testes + testes in scrotum + normal bladder and kidneys + no bowel dilatation or calcification → mechanism?
ask: Which developmental event best explains the fluid?

options.A: Failure of the gubernaculum to shorten
options.C: Meconium leak through a perforated bowel
options.D: A patent processus vaginalis allowing peritoneal fluid into the scrotum

whyNot.A: **Cryptorchidism**: testis not in the scrotum; his lie in the scrotum
whyNot.B: Gives **big bladder and hydronephrosis**; his are normal
whyNot.C: **Meconium periorchitis** gives calcification and bowel dilatation; neither is present
whyNot.E: Gives a **swollen, non-perfused testis**, not a thin rim of fluid around both

why: The **processus vaginalis** normally closes after the testis descends. If it **stays open**, **peritoneal fluid** flows into the **tunica vaginalis** and collects around the testis, forming a **communicating hydrocele**.
chain: Testis descends with the processus vaginalis
Hydrocele (often resolves in the first year)

idea.rule: A processus vaginalis that stays open gives hydrocele or an indirect inguinal hernia.
also: Wider opening lets bowel through (indirect hernia)
Hydrocele transilluminates
Acquired hydrocele in adults: infection, trauma, tumor

stem: A 64-year-old woman, gravida 4, has had years of constipation and a feeling of incomplete evacuation. She often has to press with a finger on the back wall of her vagina to pass stool. Defecation is not painful, she has no abdominal pain, and a bowel biopsy done years ago showed normal ganglion cells.
oneliner: 64F + gravida 4 + constipation + incomplete evacuation + presses posterior vaginal wall to defecate → why?
ask: Which of the following best explains her need to splint?

options.A: Lack of ganglion cells in the distal rectum

whyNot.A: **Hirschsprung disease** starts in infancy; her **biopsy showed ganglion cells**
whyNot.B: **Anismus/fissure** gives pain on defecation, not a vaginal bulge
whyNot.E: Gives a **cystocele**: an **anterior** wall bulge with urinary symptoms

answer: A weakened rectovaginal septum lets the rectum herniate
why: Childbirth and age damage the **rectovaginal septum**. The **anterior rectal wall herniates** into the posterior vagina, so stool is trapped and the patient **splints** the vaginal wall to empty.
chain: Childbirth and age weaken the septum

idea.rule: Posterior vaginal wall bulge with a need to splint means rectocele.
also: Cystocele: anterior bulge with stress incontinence
Uterine prolapse: weak cardinal and uterosacral ligaments
Risks: multiparity, forceps, obesity, chronic straining

stem: A 40-year-old man has a dull ache in the left scrotum. When he stands, a soft mass like a bag of worms appears above the left testis, enlarges with the Valsalva maneuver and disappears when he lies down. The right side is normal and the mass does not transilluminate.
oneliner: 40M + left scrotal ache + soft 'bag of worms' mass above testis enlarging on standing and Valsalva + empties supine → why left?
ask: Which of the following best explains why this condition is more common on the left?

options.A: The left testicular artery is longer
options.B: The left testicular vein drains into the left renal vein
options.C: The left inguinal canal is wider
options.D: The left testis twists more easily
options.E: The left epididymis is more often infected

whyNot.A: Arterial length does not cause **venous dilation**
whyNot.C: Canal width relates to **inguinal hernia**, not a dilated venous plexus above the testis
whyNot.D: **Torsion** causes sudden severe pain, not a dilated venous plexus
whyNot.E: **Epididymitis** is painful and febrile, with a tender epididymis

answer: Left testicular vein drains into the left renal vein
why: This is a **varicocele**, a dilated **pampiniform plexus**. The **left testicular vein enters the left renal vein at a right angle**, so renal venous pressure is transmitted to it; the **right** vein enters the **IVC** directly.
chain: Left testicular vein joins the left renal vein
Soft scrotal mass, worse on standing

idea.rule: Left-sided venous drainage into the renal vein explains left predominance of varicocele.
also: A new, non-emptying left varicocele can signal a left renal tumor or renal vein thrombosis (nephrotic syndrome)
Varicocele is a cause of male infertility (heat)
Hydrocele transilluminates, varicocele does not

stem: A 36-year-old man has a tender 1-cm nodule along the spermatic cord, which appeared 6 weeks after a vasectomy. The nodule is excised and a photomicrograph of the specimen is shown.
oneliner: 36M + tender cord nodule 6 wk after vasectomy + excised, histology shown → what process is this?
ask: Which process does the nodule represent?

whyNot.A: Affects the **testis** and is not a localized cord nodule after surgery
whyNot.B: Would show **hemosiderin and fibrin**, not histiocytes around sperm
whyNot.D: Would show **neutrophils and fever**; none described
whyNot.E: Would show **atypical cells**, not a reactive infiltrate

answer: Spermatic granuloma: foreign-body type granulomatous inflammation to leaked sperm
why: Sperm that **leak into the stroma** after the duct is cut are treated as **foreign material**. **Histiocytes and giant cells engulf them**, forming a **granuloma** that feels like a tender bead on the cord.

idea.rule: Sperm outside the duct system provoke a granulomatous response.
also: Sperm are antigenically foreign (formed after tolerance develops)
Testicular trauma or torsion can expose sperm
Tuberculosis: caseating granulomas

image.prompt: H&E photomicrograph of fibrous tissue with a granuloma of epithelioid histiocytes and a few multinucleated giant cells surrounding and engulfing pink sperm heads and tails, scattered lymphocytes, no text or labels.

stem: A 17-year-old girl has never had a period. She has normal breast development, sparse pubic and axillary hair, and a short blind-ending vagina. Ultrasound shows no uterus, and bilateral inguinal masses are found to be testes. Her karyotype is 46,XY, with high testosterone and high LH.
oneliner: 17F + primary amenorrhea + normal breasts + sparse pubic hair + blind vagina, no uterus + inguinal testes + 46,XY + high testosterone and LH → which defect?
ask: Which defect best explains her anatomy?

whyNot.A: **Virilizes at puberty** (voice, muscle, phallus) and has little breast tissue; she has breasts and a female habitus
whyNot.B: Gives **virilized genitalia in 46,XX** or salt wasting; no testes
whyNot.C: A uterus would be **present**; hers is absent
whyNot.D: Would produce **ovaries and a uterus**, not testes

answer: Androgen receptor defect: androgen insensitivity syndrome
why: Testes produce **testosterone and AMH**. **AMH regresses the uterus** (so none is found), but a **defective androgen receptor** blocks virilization, so external genitalia are female. **High LH and testosterone** reflect the failed negative feedback; the testosterone converts to estrogen and gives **breasts**.
chain: High testosterone and LH, testes in the groin

idea.rule: 46,XY with testes, no uterus and a female phenotype = androgen insensitivity.
also: 5-alpha-reductase deficiency: ambiguous genitalia, virilize at puberty
Sparse pubic and axillary hair is typical (androgen dependent)
Gonadectomy is advised later because of germ cell tumor risk

stem: A 16-year-old girl has had 7 months of deepening voice, facial hair, amenorrhea and clitoromegaly. Serum testosterone is markedly elevated, DHEAS is normal, and LH is low. Pelvic ultrasound shows a solid 6-cm right ovarian mass.
oneliner: 16F + 7 mo deepening voice, hirsutism, amenorrhea, clitoromegaly + very high testosterone + normal DHEAS + low LH + solid ovarian mass → source of androgen?
ask: Which of the following cells is the most likely source of the excess androgen?

whyNot.A: Adrenal androgen excess raises **DHEAS**, which is normal

answer: Autonomous androgen secretion by an ovarian Sertoli-Leydig cell tumor
why: A **unilateral ovarian mass** with **very high testosterone**, **normal DHEAS** (adrenal source unlikely) and **suppressed LH** (negative feedback) points to a **Sertoli-Leydig cell tumor** whose Leydig-type cells make testosterone **autonomously**.

idea.rule: High testosterone with normal DHEAS points to an ovarian, not adrenal, source.
also: Sertoli-Leydig cell tumor (young women)
Hilus (Leydig) cell tumor (postmenopausal women)
Ovarian stromal hyperthecosis
PCOS (milder rise, high LH:FSH)

stem: A 28-year-old woman has had 2 years of infrequent periods and hot flashes, and has been unable to conceive. Serum TSH, prolactin and testosterone are normal, and FSH is markedly elevated. There is no pelvic pain or galactorrhea.
oneliner: 28F + infertility + 2 y oligomenorrhea + hot flashes + normal TSH, prolactin, testosterone + high FSH → why FSH is high?
ask: Which of the following best explains the high FSH?

options.A: Depletion of follicles with loss of estrogen and inhibin feedback
options.B: Autonomous FSH secretion by a pituitary adenoma
options.D: Endometrial implants distorting the pelvic organs

whyNot.B: Would be **rare** and typically cause ovarian hyperstimulation, not hot flashes and amenorrhea
whyNot.C: Her **testosterone is normal**; PCOS has normal FSH and high LH:FSH
whyNot.D: Endometriosis gives **pelvic pain**, with normal FSH

answer: Early follicular loss lowers estrogen and inhibin, so FSH rises (primary ovarian insufficiency)
why: With follicles depleted before 40, the ovary makes **little estrogen or inhibin B**. Loss of **negative feedback** raises **FSH** (and LH), causing **hypoestrogenic** symptoms: hot flashes and amenorrhea.

idea.rule: High FSH with amenorrhea means ovarian failure.
also: Turner syndrome, fragile X premutation, autoimmune oophoritis
Chemotherapy or pelvic radiation
Classic galactosemia
Natural menopause: same pattern at about 51

stem: A 34-year-old woman, gravida 3, para 2 with two prior cesarean deliveries, delivers at 36 weeks. The placenta does not separate after 30 minutes and she bleeds 2.5 L. A hysterectomy is done and a photomicrograph of the placental attachment site is shown. Antenatal ultrasound showed a normal intrauterine pregnancy with no fibroids, and she had no pain or bleeding before labor.
oneliner: 34F G3P2 + two prior cesareans + 36 wk delivery + placenta not separating at 30 min + 2.5 L hemorrhage + hysterectomy specimen shown + no antenatal bleeding or fibroids → mechanism?
ask: Which of the following is the most likely mechanism?

options.A: Premature separation of a normally implanted placenta
options.B: Absent decidua basalis, so villi attach to the myometrium
options.D: Endometrial glands within the uterine wall

whyNot.A: Abruption causes **pain and bleeding before delivery**; here the placenta fails to separate after
whyNot.D: Adenomyosis is **glands within the myometrium**; it does not bind the placenta to the wall

answer: Placenta accreta: deficient decidua lets villi attach to or invade myometrium
why: Normally the **decidua basalis** forms a plane where the placenta separates. **Scar from prior cesareans** leaves it thin or absent, so villi **attach directly to the myometrium**, the placenta cannot separate, and **massive hemorrhage** follows.
chain: Placenta fails to separate after delivery

idea.rule: Accreta = missing decidua basalis, so villi anchor straight onto myometrium; anything that scars the endometrium raises the risk.
also: Prior cesarean (risk rises with each one)
Placenta previa over a uterine scar: highest risk
Prior curettage, myomectomy or Asherman syndrome
Deeper forms: increta (into myometrium), percreta (through serosa)

image.prompt: Microscope field of the junction between placenta and uterine wall: chorionic villi lying directly against smooth muscle bundles of the myometrium, with no decidua layer between them

stem: A 31-year-old man has been unable to father a child for 2 years. He had testicular trauma 5 years ago. Semen analysis shows sperm clumping, and testing finds antisperm antibodies in his serum. Testosterone and LH are normal.
oneliner: 31M + infertile 2 y + testicular trauma + clumped sperm + antisperm antibodies + normal testosterone → loss of function in which cell?
ask: Dysfunction of which of the following cells most likely allowed this?

whyNot.A: Make **testosterone** outside the tubules; his testosterone is normal
whyNot.B: They **go through meiosis I**; they do not form the barrier
whyNot.C: They are **products of meiosis I**, short-lived, and not barrier cells
whyNot.E: They sit in the **basal compartment outside the barrier** and do not seal it

answer: Sertoli cell tight junctions form the blood-testis barrier
why: After meiosis, sperm carry **haploid antigens the immune system never saw during development**. **Tight junctions between Sertoli cells** seal them off; trauma damages the barrier, so **antisperm antibodies** form.
chain: Haploid sperm antigens reach the immune system

idea.rule: The blood-testis barrier is made by Sertoli cell tight junctions.
also: Sertoli cells also make inhibin, AMH and androgen-binding protein
Vasectomy can cause antisperm antibodies by the same exposure
Mumps orchitis and torsion are other triggers
Immune privileged sites: testis, eye, brain

stem: A 29-year-old woman trying to conceive tracks ovulation. A urine LH surge is detected on the morning of cycle day 15. She has intercourse that day and conceives. She wants to know when a sensitive serum hCG assay will first turn positive.
oneliner: 29F + LH surge day 15 + intercourse that day + conceives → earliest day hCG detectable?
ask: How long after the LH surge will serum hCG first be detectable?

whyNot.B: Fertilized egg is still in the **fallopian tube**
whyNot.C: The embryo is still a **morula** in the tube and has not implanted
whyNot.E: By then even a urine test is positive; serum hCG turns positive **about a week earlier**

why: Ovulation follows the LH surge by about a day, fertilization follows within a day, and the blastocyst **implants about 6 days after fertilization**. The **syncytiotrophoblast** then starts making hCG, which is detectable in serum **about 1 week after fertilization**, roughly 8 days after the surge.
chain: Ovulation and fertilization about 1 day later
Serum hCG detectable about 1 week after fertilization

idea.rule: hCG is made only by trophoblast, so it appears only after implantation.
also: A test done before implantation is negative even if fertilization occurred
Ectopic implantation still makes hCG, but it rises slowly
Hydatidiform mole and choriocarcinoma (trophoblast) make very high hCG

stem: An experimental animal is given a drug that selectively blocks inhibin.
oneliner: Animal + drug that blocks inhibin → expected hormone change?

whyNot.A: Blocking a **negative feedback** signal raises FSH, not lowers it
whyNot.B: Inhibin acts on the **pituitary**, not hypothalamic GnRH
whyNot.D: LH is controlled by **testosterone**/estrogen feedback, not inhibin
whyNot.E: Leydig cells respond to **LH**, which is unchanged

why: **Inhibin** from Sertoli (or granulosa) cells **selectively inhibits FSH** release from the pituitary. Blocking it removes that brake, so **FSH rises**.

idea.rule: Inhibin is a selective negative feedback on FSH; testosterone/estrogen feed back on LH.
also: Low sperm count (Sertoli damage) gives selectively high FSH
Klinefelter: hyalinized tubules, low inhibin, high FSH
Menopause: loss of follicle inhibin raises FSH first

stem: A 27-year-old woman has serial hormone levels across a normal cycle. Estradiol rises sharply in the late follicular phase, just before the LH surge. Androstenedione is made by theca cells.
oneliner: 27F + estradiol rises late follicular phase + theca cells make androstenedione → site of estradiol production?
ask: Which cells convert androstenedione to estradiol?

whyNot.A: Theca interna cells **make** androstenedione but lack aromatase
whyNot.C: Ovarian stroma is not the site of **FSH-driven** aromatization
whyNot.E: Corpus luteum has **not formed** before ovulation

why: The **two-cell model**: **LH** acts on theca interna to make androgens, and **FSH** induces **aromatase in granulosa cells**, which convert androstenedione to **estradiol**.

idea.rule: Theca cells make the androgen, granulosa cells aromatize it: LH on theca, FSH on granulosa.
also: Aromatase deficiency: androgen piles up, estrogen low
PCOS: excess theca androgen supply
Sertoli cells use FSH-induced aromatase the same way in males

stem: A 62-year-old man has hesitancy, a weak stream, and nocturia for two years. He is afebrile. Digital rectal examination shows a diffusely enlarged, firm, rubbery, nontender prostate with a smooth surface.
oneliner: 62M + hesitancy, weak stream, nocturia + afebrile + diffusely enlarged firm nontender smooth prostate → why does the gland enlarge?

options.A: Alpha-1 receptor activation in the stroma
options.E: Chronic bacterial infection of the gland

whyNot.A: Alpha-1 activation raises **smooth muscle tone** (symptoms), but does not drive **growth**
whyNot.B: Estradiol plays a smaller supporting role; **DHT** is the main growth signal
whyNot.D: PSA is a **marker**, not a growth stimulus
whyNot.E: He is afebrile and the gland is **nontender**, against infection

why: **5-alpha-reductase** in prostate stroma converts **testosterone to DHT**, a potent androgen that drives **stromal and glandular hyperplasia** in the periurethral transition zone. The enlarged gland narrows the urethra.

idea.rule: DHT is the growth signal in BPH; 5-alpha-reductase makes it from testosterone.
also: DHT drives male-pattern hair loss
DHT forms the prostate and male external genitalia in the fetus
5-alpha-reductase deficiency: small prostate, ambiguous genitalia at birth

stem: In an experiment, a chemical is injected into the testes of rats that opens tight junctions between a particular pair of adjacent cells in the seminiferous tubule wall. The animals later make antibodies against haploid products of meiosis that enter the circulation. Those germ cell antigens first appear at puberty, long after self-tolerance is set.
oneliner: Experiment: chemical opens tight junctions in rat testis → antibodies against meiosis products appear in blood; antigens arise only after puberty → which cells form the barrier?
ask: Tight junctions between which cells form the barrier that was breached?

whyNot.A: **Leydig cells** lie **between tubules**, outside the tubule wall, and make testosterone
whyNot.B: Capillaries lie **outside the tubule wall**, so their junctions do not seal off germ cells
whyNot.C: Spermatids are the **haploid products** being hidden, not the cells that hide them
whyNot.E: **Myoid cells** contract the tubule; the tight seal around **haploid** cells is formed by another cell

why: **Sertoli cell tight junctions** form the **blood-testis barrier**, hiding **haploid germ cell antigens** that arise after tolerance forms. If it breaks, the immune system sees them as **foreign** and makes antibodies.
chain: Germ cells become haploid at puberty
Their antigens never met the immune system in infancy

idea.rule: Antigens that appear after tolerance is set must be hidden by a barrier.
also: Vasectomy or testicular trauma can expose sperm antigens (antisperm antibodies)
Lens and uveal antigens are hidden in the eye
Sympathetic ophthalmia: injury to one eye exposes antigens and both eyes inflame
Brain antigens sit behind the blood-brain barrier

stem: A 22-year-old marathon runner trains about 90 km a week and has a BMI of 17. She has had no periods for 8 months and now has pain over the left shin, where MRI shows a tibial stress fracture. LH, FSH and estradiol are all low and DEXA shows low bone density. Pregnancy test, calcium, PTH, TSH and morning cortisol are normal.
oneliner: 22F + marathon runner + BMI 17 + amenorrhea 8 months + tibial stress fracture + low LH, FSH and estradiol + low bone density + normal calcium, PTH, TSH, cortisol → which hormone deficiency explains the bone loss?
ask: Which hormone abnormality best explains her reduced bone density?

whyNot.A: Does not explain the **low LH, FSH and estradiol** or the **amenorrhea**

why: **High training volume, low BMI, amenorrhea and low LH, FSH and estradiol** mean low energy availability has suppressed hypothalamic GnRH pulses. The resulting **estrogen deficiency** removes restraint on osteoclasts, causing **low bone density and stress fractures**.
chain: Low energy availability with heavy training
Unrestrained osteoclasts: low bone density and stress fracture

idea.rule: Estrogen restrains bone resorption, so any cause of low estrogen in a young woman costs bone.
also: Female athlete triad: low energy availability, amenorrhea, low bone density
Anorexia nervosa: hypothalamic amenorrhea with bone loss
Primary ovarian insufficiency: low estrogen with high FSH
Menopause: estrogen loss speeds bone resorption
